title: Forgetting & Memory Hygiene
summary: It's tempting to keep every memory forever, but unbounded memory hurts: it inflates cost, slows retrieval, and — worse — surfaces stale or contradictory facts that make the agent wrong. Forgetting is a feature. Memory hygiene is the set of maintenance operations — eviction, decay, deduplication, and relevance filtering — that keep the store small, fresh, and precise so recall stays useful instead of becoming noise.

subtopics.title: Unbounded memory is a liability, not an asset
subtopics.explanation: A store that only ever grows costs more to hold and search, and its precision drops as old, irrelevant, and duplicated entries crowd out the good ones. Bigger is not smarter — beyond a point, more memory makes retrieval noisier and answers worse. Recognizing that unbounded memory actively harms an agent is the premise that makes every hygiene technique necessary.
subtopics.example:
# naive: never forget anything
def remember(store, fact):
    store.append(fact)   # grows forever

# symptoms as the store balloons:
#  - retrieval scans more vectors  -> slower, pricier
#  - stale/duplicate facts rank high -> noisier context
#  - contradictory facts coexist    -> wrong answers
# the fix is deliberate forgetting, not more storage

subtopics.title: Eviction bounds the store's size
subtopics.explanation: Eviction caps the store at a budget by removing entries when it's full, using a policy such as least-recently-used or lowest-importance. It keeps memory a fixed, affordable size instead of an ever-growing pile. A clear eviction policy is what guarantees cost and latency stay bounded no matter how long the agent runs.

subtopics.title: Decay lets old memories fade
subtopics.explanation: Decay weights each memory by recency (and access frequency) so newer, frequently-used facts outrank stale ones during retrieval, and long-untouched entries eventually fall below a threshold and are dropped. Unlike a hard size cap, decay is gradual and importance-aware. Time-based decay is what keeps a memory current, letting fresh facts win without an explicit overwrite.
subtopics.example:
import math, time

def decayed_score(similarity, last_used, now=None, half_life_s=86400):
    now = now or time.time()
    age = now - last_used
    recency = 0.5 ** (age / half_life_s)   # halves each half-life
    return similarity * recency            # blend relevance with freshness
# a slightly-less-similar but newer memory can now outrank a stale one

subtopics.title: Deduplication collapses repeats
subtopics.explanation: Agents re-learn the same fact many times, so dedup detects near-identical memories (by hash for exact matches or high cosine similarity for paraphrases) and keeps a single canonical copy. This stops one fact from occupying several top-k slots and skewing retrieval. Deduplication is what preserves the diversity and precision of what gets recalled.

subtopics.title: Relevance filtering and contradiction resolution
subtopics.explanation: Even after ranking, you filter out memories below a similarity threshold so junk never enters the prompt, and when two memories conflict you reconcile them — usually keeping the newest or highest-confidence and retiring the other. This prevents the agent from acting on outdated or contradictory beliefs. Filtering plus reconciliation is the final guard that keeps recalled memory trustworthy.

foundations.overview: The intuitive goal of memory — 'remember everything' — is the wrong goal. A store that only grows costs more to hold and search, and its retrieval precision falls as stale, duplicated, and contradictory entries crowd out the useful ones, so the agent's answers get worse even as its memory gets bigger. Forgetting is therefore a feature, and memory hygiene is the maintenance that implements it: eviction caps the store at a budget (e.g. LRU), decay weights memories by recency so fresh facts win and long-unused ones fade out, deduplication collapses repeated or paraphrased facts into one canonical copy, and relevance filtering plus contradiction resolution drop weak matches and reconcile conflicts by keeping the newest or highest-confidence fact. Together these keep the store small, current, and precise, so recall remains a sharp signal rather than accumulating noise.
foundations.formalDefinition: Memory hygiene is the set of maintenance operations that bound and curate an agent's memory store: eviction (size-capped removal by a policy like LRU/importance), decay (recency/frequency weighting that lets old entries fade below a threshold), deduplication (collapsing exact or near-duplicate memories), and relevance filtering with contradiction resolution (dropping sub-threshold matches and reconciling conflicts to the newest/most-confident fact).
foundations.whyItMatters: Retrieval quality, cost, and correctness all degrade with an unbounded store: more vectors to scan, more tokens injected, and stale/contradictory facts that make the agent confidently wrong. Hygiene is what keeps a long-lived agent's memory both affordable and trustworthy, so recall helps rather than hurts.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of memory like a working notebook, not an infinite archive. You cross out entries that are outdated (decay), tear out pages when it's full (eviction), avoid writing the same note twice (dedup), and, when two notes disagree, keep the latest and strike the old one (contradiction resolution) — so the notebook stays thin and reliable.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Assistants that expire preferences after a TTL, support agents that reconcile a customer's changing plan to the latest fact, vector stores that dedup on write and cap per-user memory, and recommender agents that decay old signals so recent behavior dominates.
commonUseCases: Capping per-user memory so cost and latency stay bounded
Decaying stale preferences so recent facts win at retrieval
Reconciling contradictory facts to the newest/most-confident

commonMisconceptions.myth: Keeping more memory always makes the agent smarter.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Past a point it does the opposite: stale, duplicate, and contradictory entries lower retrieval precision and raise cost, so answers get worse, not better.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Forgetting is just about saving storage space.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Its bigger payoff is correctness and precision — dropping stale/duplicate/conflicting memories keeps recall sharp; the cost savings are secondary.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Eviction and decay are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Eviction is a hard size cap that removes entries when full; decay is a gradual, recency-weighted fade that also reranks retrieval. They solve different problems and are often used together.

checkpoints.prompt: Why can an unbounded, ever-growing memory store make an agent's answers worse?
options: Stale, duplicate, and contradictory entries lower retrieval precision and can surface wrong facts
The model refuses to read large stores
Embeddings stop working past a size limit
checkpoints.explanation: Growth isn't free: old, repeated, and conflicting memories crowd out the useful ones, so top-k retrieval returns noisier and sometimes contradictory facts. That lowers precision and can make the agent confidently wrong, on top of raising cost and latency.

checkpoints.prompt: What is the key difference between eviction and decay?
options: Eviction is a hard size cap that removes entries when full; decay is a gradual recency-weighted fade that also reranks retrieval
Decay deletes instantly; eviction never deletes
Eviction only applies to vector stores
checkpoints.explanation: Eviction enforces a fixed budget by dropping entries (e.g. least-recently-used) when the store is full. Decay is gradual: it down-weights memories by age/frequency so fresh facts rank higher and long-unused ones eventually fall below a threshold. They're complementary.

checkpoints.prompt: With recency decay, which memory scores higher for retrieval?
checkpoints.code:
def score(sim, age_days, half_life=1):
    recency = 0.5 ** (age_days / half_life)
    return sim * recency
old = score(0.90, age_days=3)   # very similar but stale
new = score(0.70, age_days=0)   # less similar but fresh
print("new" if new > old else "old")
checkpoints.explanation: The stale memory's 0.90 similarity is multiplied by 0.5**3 = 0.125 (~0.1125), while the fresh one keeps 0.70 * 1 = 0.70. Decay lets the newer, slightly-less-similar memory outrank the stale one — exactly the point of recency weighting.

keyTakeaways: Unbounded memory hurts: it raises cost and latency and lowers retrieval precision as stale, duplicate, and contradictory entries pile up — forgetting is a feature.
Eviction caps the store at a budget (e.g. LRU/importance) so cost and latency stay bounded no matter how long the agent runs.
Decay weights memories by recency and frequency so fresh, useful facts win and long-untouched ones fade below a threshold.
Deduplication collapses exact and paraphrased repeats into one canonical copy so a single fact can't dominate top-k retrieval.
Relevance filtering drops weak matches and contradiction resolution keeps the newest/most-confident fact, so recalled memory stays trustworthy.
